flips.title: The First 10 Flips
flips.label: UK RESELLING PLAYBOOK
flips.disclaimer: Income is not guaranteed. Research each deal and account for all costs.

tips.hook: A resale price isn't your profit
tips.tip: Calculate what remains after purchase cost, selling fees, postage, packaging and collection costs before you buy.

tips.hook: Check SOLD prices, not asking prices
tips.tip: An active listing only tells you what a seller hopes to get. Look for credible completed sales before committing cash.

tips.hook: Set your maximum buy price first
tips.tip: Work backwards from a conservative resale value and your target profit. Walk away if the purchase price breaks the maths.

tips.hook: Don't trap all your cash in stock
tips.tip: Ten unsold items can tie up more money than you expect. Start small and measure how quickly each item sells.

tips.hook: A missing part can erase your margin
tips.tip: Check model numbers, cables, accessories and condition before buying second-hand products.

tips.hook: Photos should show the faults too
tips.tip: Clear photos of condition and defects reduce misunderstandings and help buyers decide confidently.

tips.hook: The cheapest listing isn't the best flip
tips.tip: A low purchase price means little without buyer demand, resale evidence and a workable selling margin.
Fuel, travel time, parking and courier costs all change the true profit of a resale deal.

tips.hook: Do the postage maths before listing
tips.tip: Measure and weigh the item before setting a delivery price. Bulky products can surprise you.
Track each item's purchase price, date, condition and selling costs, so you know what actually worked.

tips.hook: Give slow stock a review date
tips.tip: Set a point to revisit the price or selling platform rather than leaving unsold items forgotten in storage.
A repeatable sourcing and pricing process is more useful than buying random bargains and hoping they sell.

adhd.title: The ADHD Money Reset
adhd.label: MONEY & LIFE ADMIN TOOLKIT
adhd.disclaimer: Organisation resource, not financial or medical advice.

tips.hook: Start with the next three bills
tips.tip: You don't have to reorganise your entire financial life today. Find the next three bills and their due dates first.
Check what is available, note incoming money, find the next bills, flag anything urgent and take one action.
Put payment reminders somewhere you will actually see them rather than relying on memory alone.
When the admin feels too big, choose one next step: set a reminder, find a letter or contact a provider.
Identify urgent or priority bills before spending time perfecting budget categories and spreadsheets.
Write down your recurring payments and review whether you still use them. Look at dates and amounts together.
A simple routine you can restart is often more useful than a complicated budget you abandon after one week.

tips.hook: Give every bill a due date
tips.tip: A named bill with a due date and a next action is easier to handle than an unnamed worry in your head.
If your income changes, avoid planning essential bills around the best-case amount.
A short script can make it easier to contact a provider about a missed payment instead of avoiding the issue.
Keep one visible page for bills, subscriptions and deadlines rather than scattering the details across apps.

tips.hook: Restarting is part of the plan
tips.tip: An organisation system should still work after you've missed a week. Start again with the next actionable step.

hospital.title: Hospital to Home
hospital.label: ENGLAND FAMILY ORGANISER
hospital.kind: Hospital discharge family planning toolkit for adults in England
hospital.disclaimer: Independent organisation aid, not NHS-affiliated or medical advice. Follow the treating team's instructions.

tips.tip: Ask the hospital team who is coordinating the discharge plan and where your family can direct outstanding questions.
Record who is collecting the person, how they will get inside, and which arrangements still need confirming.
Ask the clinical team about medicine changes, written instructions and whom to contact if there are questions later.

tips.hook: Keep follow-up dates in one place
tips.tip: Record the appointment, location, contact details and who will arrange transport or accompany the patient.
Check with the discharge team whether any recommended equipment or home support is needed and confirmed.
Keep key contacts, arrangements and unresolved questions together so family members work from the same information.
Create a simple rota for practical tasks such as shopping, transport and phone calls, respecting the patient's wishes.

tips.hook: Ask who to call with questions
tips.tip: Before leaving, make sure the patient knows which clinical service to contact about concerns after discharge.
Confirm how the patient is getting home and any practical access concerns before the planned discharge time.
Write down who is handling appointments, essentials and follow-up calls to reduce duplicated or forgotten tasks.
Only share the discharge organiser with the patient's permission and store sensitive information carefully.
A concise list of questions helps you use discharge conversations to clarify the practical plan rather than guess.
